issues.legal_issue: A tenant admitted to land under an agreement made pursuant to a statutory exception does not acquire occupancy rights merely because the exception’s twelve-year period expires, and the agreement is not thereby superseded.
material_facts: The land was non-private land in an estate covered by the statutory scheme.
The landholder had obtained a final decree establishing that the earlier tenant had no occupancy right, and no tenant had acquired an occupancy right before the land became subject to the scheme.
The landholder admitted the tenant to possession under lease agreements made during the statutory twelve-year period.
The parties accepted that the facts satisfied the requirements of the statutory exception.
issues.conclusion: The exception governed notwithstanding the general occupancy-right provision, and the expiry of its twelve-year period did not itself terminate or supersede the agreed lease terms or give the tenant an occupancy right.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 6(1) and 8(5) of the Madras Estates Land Act, section 6(1) is subject to the Act, whereas section 8(5) operates notwithstanding anything contained in the Act. If both provisions apply, section 8(5) governs. Its plain language permits admission on agreed terms, including the lease period, and does not make the agreement expire or become superseded when the twelve-year period ends. The Court followed Executive Officer v. L.K. Ganapathi Thevar, (1955) 2 M.L.J. 112, and Sri Navaneethaswaraswami Devasthanam Sikki v. P. Swaminatha Pillai, I.L.R. (1958) Mad. 921; it distinguished Muminia Damudu v. Datla Papayyaraju Garu, A.I.R. 1944 Mad. 136, Korda Atchanna v. Jayanti Seetharamaswami, A.I.R. 1950 Mad. 357, Thota Seshayya v. Madabushi Vedanta Narasimhacharyulu, I.L.R. (1955) Mad. 1151, and Vadranam Ramchandrayya v. Madabhushi Ranganavakamma, (1957) 2 Andhra Weekly Reports 114, as not deciding the question at issue.

rule.if: occupancy_right_claim and land_in_covered_estate and land_is_not_private and qualifying_prior_decree and no_prior_occupancy_right and tenant_admitted_during_window_on_agreed_terms

predicates.occupancy_right_claim: A tenant claims a right to remain in possession based on a statutory occupancy right.
predicates.land_in_covered_estate: The land is within an estate covered by the applicable land-tenure scheme.
predicates.land_is_not_private: The land is not classified as the landholder’s private land.
predicates.qualifying_prior_decree: The landholder had obtained a final decree establishing that a tenant had no occupancy right before the relevant statutory cutoff.
predicates.no_prior_occupancy_right: No tenant had acquired an occupancy right before the land became subject to the statutory scheme.
predicates.tenant_admitted_during_window_on_agreed_: The landholder admitted the tenant to possession during the specified statutory window on terms agreed with the tenant.

issues.definition: When a tenant claims an occupancy right in covered non-private land, and the qualifying prior decree, absence of an earlier occupancy right, and admission on agreed terms during the statutory window are present, expiry of that window alone does not create the claimed right or supersede the agreed terms.

issues.legal_issue: A person qualifies as a cultivating tenant under the amended definition only if the person or a family member contributes physical labour to cultivation; supervision or management alone is insufficient.
material_facts: The tenant claimed protection from eviction as a cultivating tenant.
The land was cultivated solely with hired labour.
Neither the tenant nor any member of the tenant’s family took part in the cultivation operations.
The tenant’s claimed involvement amounted to supervision rather than physical labour.
issues.conclusion: The tenant was not a cultivating tenant under the amended definition and could not claim the protection available to cultivating tenants.
issues.legal_principle: The definition of “cultivating tenant” in the Madras Cultivating Tenants Protection Act, 1955, as amended by the addition of its explanation, requires personal cultivation involving the tenant’s or a family member’s physical labour. Physical labour entails physical strain and the use of muscles and sinews; mere supervision, keeping accounts, or distributing wages is insufficient. The Court relied on Mohamed Abubucker Lebbai v. The Zamindar of Ettayapuram Estate, Koilapatti, (1961) 1 M.L.J. 256, and S.N. Sundalaimuthi Chettiar v. Palaniyandayan, (1966) 1 S.C.R. 450.

predicates.cultivating_tenant_protection_claim: A tenant seeks protection from eviction on the basis of being a cultivating tenant.
predicates.cultivation_done_only_by_hired_labour: The land was cultivated solely by hired workers.
predicates.claimant_and_family_performed_no_physica: Neither the claimant nor a member of the claimant’s family contributed physical labour to cultivating the land.

issues.definition: A tenant seeking cultivating-tenant protection does not qualify when hired workers alone cultivate the land and neither the tenant nor the tenant’s family contributes physical labour.

issues.legal_issue: A determination firmly made by an appellate court before remand binds the trial court and a later bench hearing the appeal, but it may be challenged in an appeal to the Supreme Court from the final judgment.
material_facts: An earlier appellate judgment expressly considered and finally rejected the tenant’s claim to an occupancy right.
The case was remanded for trial of other issues.
After remand, the trial court and the later appellate bench treated the earlier determination as binding.
The tenant challenged that determination in an appeal to the Supreme Court against the final judgment.
issues.conclusion: The trial court and the later appellate bench were bound by the earlier determination, but the tenant could challenge it in the Supreme Court appeal from the final judgment.
issues.legal_principle: A determination finally made on an issue in an earlier stage binds the court conducting proceedings after remand and a later bench hearing the appeal. However, the correctness of that determination may be challenged in an appeal to the Supreme Court against the final judgment. The Court relied on Satyadhyan Ghosal v. Sm. Deorajin Debi, [1960] 3 S.C.R. 590.

predicates.appeal_to_supreme_court_from_final_judgm: The matter is an appeal to the Supreme Court from a final judgment entered after an earlier appellate decision remanded the case.
predicates.earlier_appellate_decision_firmly_resolv: An earlier appellate decision expressly and finally resolved the issue before the case was remanded for other proceedings.

issues.definition: When a final-judgment appeal follows a remand and an earlier appellate decision firmly resolved an issue, that decision binds the courts below but may still be challenged in the Supreme Court appeal.
